title: Robust and Adaptive Optimization (Bertsimas, den Hertog; Dynamic Ideas 2022): publisher's book page (purpose, six parts, distinguishing characteristics)
contribution: The publisher's page of Robust and Adaptive Optimization (2022) states, in the co-authors' 'we', three structural choices and what each is chosen against: RO and ARO unified, with ARO before nonlinear RO because ARO solves RO problems ('a fact not fully recognized earlier'); nonlinear RO by concave vs convex uncertainty instead of robust conic optimization; applications guided by a Dantzig quotation in the unread preface.
problem_entry: {RO; LO in Parts I-II, CP in Parts III-IV, SD and AP in Part VI} Purpose: 'to provide a unified, insightful, and original treatment of robust and adaptive optimization'. The entry is the book's architecture, which the page comments on as 'distinguishing characteristics in our selection of the particular structure of the book' (p. 1).
key_idea: Three stated choices (p. 1): (1) RO and ARO for LO in Parts I-II, then RO for nonlinear optimization in Parts III-IV, 'as opposed to presenting RO first and then ARO', because 'ARO offers new and very effective ways to solve RO problems'; (2) nonlinear RO 'using concave and convex uncertainty respectively, as opposed to treating robust conic optimization', with no reason given; (3) the applications of Part VI 'guided by the quote of George Dantzig at the beginning of the preface' (the quotation is not on the page). Parts: I linear RO and its uncertainty sets; II modelling, exact and approximate algorithms for ARO; III nonlinear RO, concave uncertainty; IV nonlinear RO, convex uncertainty; V theory of distributionally RO and ARO; VI applications incl. queueing theory, auction design, option pricing, energy unit commitment (p. 1). [inferred] Order: the LP case with ARO first, then the nonlinear cases, distributional theory, applications last.
assumptions: n/a for a book page: model classes named only (linear RO with uncertainty sets, ARO, nonlinear RO with concave or convex uncertainty, distributionally robust RO and ARO); no uncertainty model, data or tractability assumption is stated (p. 1).
proof_devices: n/a: no device, theorem or bound named; the one analytic claim, that ARO gives new and very effective ways to solve RO problems, is stated without evidence (p. 1)

Part II promises 'exact and approximate algorithms for ARO' (p. 1); the third-party chapter list shows decision rules, 'RO as an Approximation to Two-Stage ARO' and a cutting-plane chapter (B012 p. 1, title only)
experiments: n/a: no instances, solvers or numbers; the applications are chosen under Dantzig's quotation (p. 1).
positioning: Two unattributed contrasts: 'presenting RO first and then ARO' and 'treating robust conic optimization'. No author, book or paper is named, so which treatments are meant is not stated; 'original' and 'not fully recognized earlier' set the book against the field at large (p. 1).
writing: Purpose sentence on the template of his book pages: 'unified, insightful, and modern' (Optimization over Integers, B006 p. 1), 'unified, insightful, modern and entertaining' (The Analytics Edge, B017 p. 1), here 'original' [02 W1]. Each characteristic is a choice plus an 'as opposed to' contrast, one of three with a reason [02 W7]; co-authors' first person plural (p. 1). Reading notes, not findings: a double full stop after the purpose sentence, an unmatched '(' before the first characteristic, the byline 'Den Hertog' (p. 1; all on the live page).
limits_future: No limits stated; no prerequisites, course, or account of which parts are the authors' own research (the Optimization over Integers and Analytics Edge pages name MIT classes, B006 p. 1, B017 p. 1). Not named in the parts list: data-driven uncertainty sets, robust discrete optimization, the price of robustness, simulation-based (HS) RO; the third-party list adds 'Choosing Uncertainty Sets and Their Parameters' and 'Robust Discrete Optimization' to Part I and names no price or simulation-based RO (B012 p. 1, title only). Book body and preface not open; the Dantzig quotation was not seen and is not supplied.

method_links.note: The book step of the RO programme, written with a colleague and published by his own press [01 §1.9; 04 B.7]; the page adds the organising choices and the reason for one of them; no course named.

Framing only: linear RO and its sets first, then ARO with exact and approximate algorithms, then nonlinear RO split by how the uncertainty enters. [inferred] The concave/convex split matches where exact counterparts end: for constraints convex in the uncertainty a tractable exact reformulation is out of reach in general (S283 p. 3, card s17). The page gives no reason for the split.

title: Review of Robust and Adaptive Optimization by Thibaut Cuvelier, developpez.com (2 December 2022, in French), with the site's chapter list
contribution: A signed French review (Thibaut Cuvelier, developpez.com, 2 December 2022) reads the RO book as pragmatic (computing time in practice over complexity class), strong on modelling and algorithms, and unusually explicit about the link with probability; the entry also carries the publisher's summary and a third-party list of 27 chapter titles in six parts. Peer view, never Bertsimas's voice.
problem_entry: {RO; DRO; SD and AP through the applications part} The reviewer's framing: once an optimal solution is found, how robust is it if not every parameter turns out as planned (a slightly longer trip, slightly dearer electricity)? RO finds solutions that work well for a whole range of parameter values rather than one value ('choix plus classique'); RO is the book's only subject ('l'objet unique de cet ouvrage') (p. 1).
key_idea: The reviewer's reading (p. 1): a very pragmatic approach in which computing times in practice matter more than an abstract complexity class; RO theory, adaptive or distributional, well covered from the foundations in duality to equivalences between robust and adaptive optimization ('des équivalences entre optimisation robuste et adaptative'); an emphasis on modelling (a whole part of applications) and on solution algorithms, classical or less so; and, as the distinguishing feature, stochastic thinking: characterizations of constraint-violation probability and stochastic quantities approximated by RO techniques, beyond the usual justification of ellipsoidal sets.
assumptions: n/a for a review. Intended reader: an OR practitioner who knows optimization without uncertainty (linear, convex, integer problems) but has not necessarily met uncertainty; site tag 'Public visé : Intermédiaire'. The site's edition data: Dynamic Ideas, 600 pages, 1st edition, 2 January 2022, ISBN-10 1733788522, ISBN-13 9781733788526, which agrees with note 01 §1.9 (p. 1).
proof_devices: the reviewer names duality foundations, RO-ARO equivalences and probability results (violation probabilities; stochastic quantities approximated by RO) without describing any device or theorem (p. 1)

contents list, title only (a third party, unchecked against the print): six headings that read as the part titles of B011, in order, with 27 chapters: Robust Linear Optimization 5, Adaptive Linear Optimization 7, Robust Nonlinear Optimization with Concave Uncertainty 3, ... with Convex Uncertainty 3, Distributionally Robust Optimization 2, The Impact of Robust Optimization 7; 'RCQO' is not expanded (p. 1)

[inferred, title only] the adaptive part is the largest and holds 'The Cutting Plane Method' and 'The Art of Robust and Adaptive Modeling'; 'RO as an Approximation to Two-Stage ARO' and 'An ARO Approach to Robust NLO' carry B011's stated reason (p. 1)

titles that match carded papers by subject only: Pareto Robustly Optimal Solutions ~ S348 (card s20); Guarantees for Concave Uncertainty ~ S215 (card s13); A Unified Framework for Convex Uncertainty ~ S283 (card s17); RO as an Approximation to Two-Stage ARO ~ S134 (card s07) and S176 (card s2-06); ARO for the Unit Commitment Problem ~ S006 (card c13) (p. 1)
experiments: None reported. The reviewer's only statement on evaluation: computing time in practice matters more than an abstract complexity class (p. 1).
positioning: The reviewer: the book differs from other treatments of RO ('d'autres traitements de l'optimisation robuste') by its handling of stochastic thinking; other treatments often limit the link to justifying ellipsoidal sets; no other book is named (p. 1). Cross-check: this feature is not among the authors' three stated characteristics (B011 p. 1), and the review mentions none of those (ARO-first order, concave/convex organisation, Dantzig).
writing: Four short paragraphs, descriptive and appreciative; 'Néanmoins' sets the theory coverage against the emphasis on modelling and algorithms and is not a criticism; reading note: 'l'auteur' in the singular for a book with two authors (p. 1).
limits_future: No limitation or criticism is stated. Strengths named: the pragmatic stance, theory coverage, modelling and algorithms, the probability link, and 'Chaque chapitre a une bibliographie imposante et variée.' (p. 1). Route to 05-peer-critique.md §4 as a positive, signed and dated reception item; it does not bear on any of the RO critiques 05 records (among them Pareto efficiency of budgeted optima, the 2006 inventory formulation, affine policies, robust queueing). No chapter title names a price, data-driven sets as such, or simulation-based RO (absence from titles only). The site's news item linking to the entry was not read.

method_links.note: Peer view, not his voice: an outside reader finds the RO book judging tractability by computing time in practice, not by complexity class. The same stance is a stated principle of the ML book, 'Practical tractability not polynomial solvability leads to real world impact.' (B009 p. 1), which the reviewer does not cite.

Peer view: the link with probability is 'rarement aussi explicite et détaillé' (constraint-violation probabilities; stochastic quantities approximated by RO). Outside support for the practice side of T3, three years after the 2019 ML principle (B009 p. 1); that principle concerns ML and is not contradicted.

title: Queueing Theory: Classical and Modern Methods (Bertsimas, Gamarnik; Dynamic Ideas 2022): publisher's book page (structure, Parts I-V)
contribution: The publisher's page of Queueing Theory: Classical and Modern Methods (2022, with his former student Gamarnik) gives only the five-part structure: single and multi-server queues, single and multiclass networks, asymptotic methods, optimization in queueing networks, and the probability machinery in an appendix.
problem_entry: {SD; optimization in Part IV, its class not stated} A queueing-theory text spanning 'Classical and Modern Methods' (title); the page states the structure only, with no purpose or audience (p. 1).
key_idea: Parts (p. 1): I single and multi-server queues; II single and multiclass queueing networks (MQNETs); III asymptotic methods: networks in heavy traffic, large deviations, call centers, queues in space, the supermarket model; IV 'the use of optimization in queueing networks'; V Markov chains and processes, Brownian motion and weak convergence 'in the Appendix'. [inferred from the order] Single stations, then networks, then limit regimes; optimization after the analysis, one part of five; the probabilistic toolkit in an appendix, as Optimization over Integers puts its background in appendices A-B (B007 p. 4).
assumptions: n/a: the page names model families only (single and multi-server queues; single and multiclass networks) (p. 1).
proof_devices: n/a on the page: the tools named are Part III's asymptotic methods and Part V's Markov chains, Brownian motion and weak convergence; what Part IV's optimization contains (achievable region, fluid relaxations, LP or SDP formulations) is not stated (p. 1)
positioning: The title pairs 'Classical' with 'Modern'; no rival named, no novelty claimed; the publisher's text, with no first person (p. 1). Part III names topics of his own earlier SD work, e.g. large deviations (cards s04 S177, s4-01 S819), by name only; whether 'queues in space' includes spatial models such as SW6's dynamic routing is not said.
writing: Five lines, each a part numeral and a verb; the first four verbs in order (describes, treats, introduces, outlines) are those of the RAO page (B011 p. 1), a press template; no purpose sentence and no section on philosophy or distinguishing characteristics, unlike the RAO, Optimization over Integers and ML pages (B011, B006, B009) (p. 1).
limits_future: The page claims nothing beyond the structure; purpose, audience, course and preface are absent (p. 1); no other open part was found (works.json note). Robust queueing (his 2010s line [01 §1.3]; critique 05 §4.5) is not named, while the RO book's third-party list has 'Robust Queueing Theory' (B012 p. 1) [inferred from two summaries]. His own books page describes the book only through Parts III-V (B008 p. 1). Methods 1 and 7: not determinable, since Part IV's content is not stated.

title: The Analytics Edge in Healthcare (Bertsimas, Orfanoudaki, Wiberg; Dynamic Ideas 2025): publisher's book page and the authors' book site (aims, chapter list)
contribution: The publisher's page and the authors' site of The Analytics Edge in Healthcare (2025, with his former students Orfanoudaki and Wiberg) give its aims (clinical practice, foundations, recent advances), a joint stance that analytics is synergistic with medical expertise, and a 22-chapter list: 11 method chapters, each taught through one clinical example and closing with a decision-making group, 9 case studies and 2 summary tables.
problem_entry: {AP (healthcare), ML, DA; IO or LO through the optimization chapter} 'Analytics is transforming healthcare operations, empowering medical professionals and administrators to leverage data and models to make better decisions.' (pp. 1, 2). Tagline: machine learning and optimization 'transform clinical and operational decisions' (p. 2). Three goals: the edge analytics can bring to daily practice; 'a broad yet concise overview of the technical foundations of the field'; recent advances 'from interpretable risk scores to fair allocation policies' through applications developed with leading medical centers. Audiences: medical students, doctors and nurses, hospital executives and administrators, analytics students and researchers (p. 2).
key_idea: Stance: analytics is 'not in conflict with medical expertise, but synergistic with it' (p. 2). Structure (p. 2): Part I Methods, 11 chapters in four groups (supervised: classification, regression, survival analysis; unsupervised: clustering, missing-data imputation; deep learning: neural networks, NLP, multimodal data; learning for decision-making: optimization with radiologist scheduling, prescriptive methods with personalized diabetes care, fairness with transplantation policy), each 'through the lens of a real clinical example'; Part II nine integrated case studies (emergency surgery, length of stay, inpatient flow, heart disease, coronary treatments, chemotherapy regimens, organ allocation, bias in trauma care, COVID-19); Part III two summary tables (methods; evaluation metrics). [inferred, title only] Prediction first, decision last; optimization is one chapter of eleven, taught through an operations example.
assumptions: n/a: the data claim is care 'learned from the records of millions of patients' (p. 2); p. 1 names multimodal models on electronic health records (p. 1).
experiments: n/a: no results; chapter 22 summarises evaluation metrics, and whether they are prediction or decision metrics is not known (p. 2).
positioning: Analytics as a complement to clinicians; applications 'developed with leading medical centers', i.e. partners as validation (p. 2). The site lists Bertsimas as Boeing Professor, Associate Dean of Business Analytics and faculty director of the Master of Business Analytics at MIT, without his Vice Provost role (reading note) (p. 2). It reuses the 2016 brand The Analytics Edge (B017 p. 1; B008 p. 1).
writing: Each Part I title pairs a method with a clinical example; a four-number summary (22 chapters, 3 parts, 9 case studies, 11 classes of methods) (p. 2); practical, promotional register ('this exciting field', p. 1). Reading notes, not findings: 'broad yet concise' in the goals vs 'broad yet rigorous' in objective II (p. 2); p. 1 describes two parts, p. 2 three; the press is in 'Boston, Massachusetts' on the site (p. 2) and in 'Belmont, Massachusetts' on B008 p. 1.
limits_future: No limits stated. The book was not read: its PDF, 'freely available for academic and personal use', is e-mailed only after a request form, which was not used (p. 2). By title, chapters 1-8 are learning methods without a decision; Part II mixes prediction titles (13, 15) with decision or policy titles (14, 16, 17, 18, 20); no title names robust optimization, causal inference or generative AI. Some titles match carded programmes by subject only: organ allocation (S476, card c2-07), hospital flow and length of stay (S617, card c38), COVID-19 (05 §5.2), chemotherapy regimens (DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2015.2363) (p. 2). Cross-check: the 2016 Analytics Edge is organised by applications and puts problems and data first (B017 p. 1); here Part I is organised by methods.

Within C21's scope: 'interpretable risk scores' among the recent advances and 'Interpretable Analytics' in case 13's title; the three deep-learning chapters teach detection, language and outcome prediction, not treatment choice ([inferred], title only).

The book's own philosophy statement, if any, is not open.

title: Dimitris Bertsimas's own books pages: Published Books on dbertsim.mit.edu (2026) and Books on his old MIT homepage (2017)
contribution: His own books pages (2026: eight books; 2017: four) present every book as a Dynamic Ideas edition, with descriptions that are mostly the publishers' sentences verbatim (19 of 21 on p. 1); the old page adds a four-part map of Optimization over Integers in the co-authors' voice (algorithms built on algebra and geometry; mixed integer and robust discrete optimization for real problems that mix continuous and discrete variables and carry uncertainty), whose chapter ranges contradict the printed contents.
problem_entry: {LO IO RO SD ML DA AP: all eight books} How he lists and describes his books on his own sites, and which dates and publishers he gives (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: p. 1 (2026): eight books, newest first by listed year except that Optimization Over Integers (2005) follows Data, Models and Decisions (2004); every book 'Dynamic Ideas, Belmont, Massachusetts'; Introduction to Linear Optimization given as 2008, Data, Models and Decisions as the 2nd edition of 2004 (p. 1). p. 2 (2017): four books with months; Introduction to Linear Optimization as 'Dynamic Ideas and Athena Scientific, Belmont, Massachusetts, March, 2008.' (p. 2). Cross-check (scripted): 19 of 21 description sentences on p. 1 are verbatim on publisher pages (B002 p. 3, B006, B010, B014, B017, B019); the queueing sentence condenses Parts III-V of B013, and the RO sentence recasts B011's purpose sentence; the ML description is the older publisher summary (B010 p. 1), not the current page (B009). p. 2 adds a four-part map of Optimization over Integers: Part I ch. 1-5 formulations and relaxations; Part II ch. 6-8 algebra and geometry, the geometry 'a key feature of the book'; Part III ch. 9-11 algorithms based on Part II; Part IV ch. 12-13 mixed integer and robust discrete optimization (p. 2).
proof_devices: n/a: the only analytic stance is the dependency that the map of Optimization over Integers states, algebra and geometry (Part II) as 'the building blocks for developing algorithms' (Part III) (p. 2)
experiments: n/a: the ML claim gives time scales (seconds/minutes; minutes/hours) without numbers or a test (p. 1).
positioning: Books defined by their departure from earlier books: 'This book represents a departure from existing textbooks.' (Data, Models and Decisions) and 'We depart from earlier treatments of integer optimization ...' (Optimization over Integers) (pp. 1-2); 'original' for the ML and RO books; no rival named (pp. 1-2).
writing: Adjective template, counted on p. 1 [02 W1]: 'unified' in four descriptions (RO, The Analytics Edge, linear optimization, integers), 'insightful' in three (RO, The Analytics Edge, integers), 'modern' in three (The Analytics Edge, linear optimization, integers), 'original' in two (ML, RO). Reading notes, not findings: 'Holly Wilberg' (p. 1; the authors' site has Wiberg, B019 p. 2); 'oulines' and 'continous' (p. 2); the label 'Co-author:' over two names (p. 1).
limits_future: Use for dating and self-presentation. Both pages date Introduction to Linear Optimization by its 2008 Dynamic Ideas edition, not the 1997 Athena Scientific first edition (B002 p. 1), and Data, Models and Decisions by its 2004 second edition, not the 2000 first [01 §1.9]: date the books by first edition. Contradiction, kept: the chapter ranges of Optimization over Integers on p. 2 (approximation algorithms in Part III = chapters 9-11; Part IV = chapters 12 and 13) disagree with the printed contents (approximation algorithms chapter 12, mixed integer optimization 13, robust discrete optimization 14; B007 pp. 3-4). Neither page carries preface text.

method_links.note: Every book appears as a Dynamic Ideas edition, his own press, including the two first published elsewhere (Athena Scientific 1997; the 2000 first edition of Data, Models and Decisions [01 §1.9]); the 2017 page gives 'Dynamic Ideas and Athena Scientific, Belmont, Massachusetts, March, 2008.' Courses are named on the publisher pages (B006, B014, B017), not here.

Stated jointly: the ML book's description promises the protocol's outcomes in one sentence: solutions in seconds/minutes, certification of optimality in minutes/hours, and wins over classical heuristics out of sample. The book provides an original treatment of machine learning (ML) using convex, robust and mixed integer optimization that leads to solutions to central ML problems at large scale that can be found in seconds/minutes, can be certified to be optimal in minutes/hours, and outperform classical heuristic approaches in out-of-sample experiments.
